claim: Decades of research investigating the inter-brain neural relationship have focused on the similarity in neural activity across brains.
source: Decades of research investigating this relationship have focused on the similarity in neural activity across brains.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature spanning diverse species and methodologies

claim: Nearly all research on inter-brain relationships has assessed similarity using measures related to either correlation or coherence.
source: Commonly, similarity was assessed using measures related to either correlation (Dikker et al., 2014; Kawasaki et al., 2013; King-Casas et al., 2005; Kingsbury et al., 2019; Kinreich et al., 2017; Levy et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2017; Montague et al., 2002; Piazza et al., 2020; Silbert et al., 2014; Spiegelhalder et al., 2014; Stephens et al., 2010; Stolk et al., 2014; Tomlin et al., 2006; Zadbood et al., 2017; Zhang and Yartsev, 2019) or coherence (Cui et al., 2012; Dikker et al., 2017; Dumas et al., 2010; Goldstein et al., 2018; Levy et al., 2017; Lindenberger et al., 2009; Montague et al., 2002; Mu et al., 2017; Stolk et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2020; Yun et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by extensive citations to prior literature using correlation and coherence measures

claim: The difference in neural activity between brains has remained unexplored in inter-brain relationship research.
source: However, one aspect of the inter-brain neural relationship has remained unexplored: the difference in neural activity between brains.
evidence: Based on review of existing literature showing focus on similarity measures rather than difference measures

claim: Inter-brain difference is more than simply a lack of inter-brain correlation.
source: We reasoned that inter-brain difference is more than simply a lack of inter-brain correlation.
evidence: Based on logical reasoning about the information content of difference dynamics

claim: The detailed dynamics of the difference between brains could contain information not captured by measures of inter-brain similarity such as correlation.
source: Specifically, the detailed dynamics of the difference between brains could contain information not captured by measures of inter-brain similarity such as correlation.
evidence: Based on logical reasoning about information content; later supported by experimental observations

claim: Egyptian fruit bats (Rousettus aegyptiacus) are known for their high level of sociality.
source: We applied this approach to neural activity simultaneously recorded from socially interacting Egyptian fruit bats (Rousettus aegyptiacus), a mammalian species known for its high level of sociality (Herzig-Straschil and Robinson, 1978; Harten et al., 2018; Prat et al., 2015; Prat et al., 2016; Prat et al., 2017; Omer et al., 2018; Cvikel et al., 2015; Egert-Berg et al., 2018; Kwiecinski and Griffiths, 1999).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature on bat social behavior

claim: The frontal cortex is implicated in social cognition in rodents, bats, non-human primates, and humans.
source: Our recordings targeted the frontal cortex (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), a region implicated in social cognition in rodents, bats, non-human primates, and humans (Adolphs, 2001; Amodio and Frith, 2006; Cao et al., 2018; Chang et al., 2013; Eliades and Miller, 2017; Forbes and Grafman, 2010; Haroush and Williams, 2015; Kingsbury et al., 2019; Liang et al., 2018; Miller et al., 2015; Nummela et al., 2017; Ong et al., 2021; Pearson et al., 2014; Rose et al., 2021; Rudebeck et al., 2008; Tremblay et al., 2017; Zhang and Yartsev, 2019; Zhou et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by extensive citations to prior literature on frontal cortex function across species

claim: Wireless extracellular neural recording was performed simultaneously from pairs of bats.
source: We performed wireless extracellular neural recording simultaneously from pairs of bats.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental method performed

claim: Four types of neural signals were recorded: local field potential (LFP) power in the 30–150 Hz and 1–29 Hz bands, multiunit activity, and single unit activity.
source: We recorded four types of neural signals: local field potential (LFP) power in the 30–150 Hz and 1–29 Hz bands (previously identified as relevant frequency bands in bat frontal cortical LFP [Zhang and Yartsev, 2019]), multiunit activity, and single unit activity (Materials and methods).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental measurements performed

claim: The 30–150 Hz and 1–29 Hz frequency bands were previously identified as relevant frequency bands in bat frontal cortical LFP.
source: local field potential (LFP) power in the 30–150 Hz and 1–29 Hz bands (previously identified as relevant frequency bands in bat frontal cortical LFP [Zhang and Yartsev, 2019])
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: The 30–150 Hz LFP frequency range exhibits strong inter-brain correlation in bats.
source: The analyses in the main text focus on 30–150 Hz LFP power, as previous work has shown that this frequency range exhibits strong inter-brain correlation in bats (Zhang and Yartsev, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: In one-chamber sessions, pairs of bats behaved freely and interacted with each other inside a chamber.
source: In one experiment, pairs of bats behaved freely and interacted with each other inside a chamber ('one-chamber sessions'; Figure 1A).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental condition; illustrated in Figure 1A

claim: In two-chambers sessions, the same bats freely behaved in separate, identical chambers.
source: In the second set of experiments, the same bats freely behaved in separate, identical chambers ('two-chambers sessions'; Figure 1B).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental condition; illustrated in Figure 1B

claim: There were three types of two-chambers sessions: (1) two bats each freely behaving in isolation; (2) two bats each freely behaving in the presence of identical auditory stimuli; (3) two bats each freely behaving and interacting with a different partner in separate chambers.
source: There were three types of two-chambers sessions: (1) two bats each freely behaving in isolation; (2) two bats each freely behaving in the presence of identical auditory stimuli (playback of bat calls); (3) two bats each freely behaving and interacting with a different partner in separate chambers.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental conditions

claim: Neural activity shows a high degree of similarity between brains in one-chamber sessions.
source: Plotting the neural activity of the two bats in one-chamber sessions shows a high degree of similarity between brains (Figure 1C), which is not the case for two-chambers sessions (Figure 1D), as demonstrated previously (Zhang and Yartsev, 2019).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1C and supported by citation to prior work

claim: Neural activity does not show a high degree of similarity between brains in two-chambers sessions.
source: Plotting the neural activity of the two bats in one-chamber sessions shows a high degree of similarity between brains (Figure 1C), which is not the case for two-chambers sessions (Figure 1D), as demonstrated previously (Zhang and Yartsev, 2019).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1D and supported by citation to prior work

claim: In one-chamber sessions, the mean component had much larger variance than the difference component.
source: Figure 1E shows the mean and difference activity components for the example session from Figure 1C. Visualizing the two components side-by-side, two relationships are immediately apparent. First, the mean component had much larger variance than the difference component.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1E for example session

claim: In one-chamber sessions, the difference component evolved over time at much faster timescales than the mean component.
source: Second, the difference component evolved over time at much faster timescales than the mean component. This is even more apparent when examining the autocorrelations of the mean and difference components (Figure 1G), where the narrower autocorrelation of the difference indicates that it varied faster than the mean.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1G for example session

claim: In two-chambers sessions, the variances of the mean and difference components were comparable.
source: In contrast, the two-chambers sessions showed a very different picture. Figure 1F shows the mean and difference components for the example session from Figure 1D. Here, the variances of the two components were comparable, and so were their timescales, which is also apparent from their comparable autocorrelations shown in Figure 1H.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1H for example session

claim: In two-chambers sessions, the timescales of the mean and difference components were comparable.
source: In contrast, the two-chambers sessions showed a very different picture. Figure 1F shows the mean and difference components for the example session from Figure 1D. Here, the variances of the two components were comparable, and so were their timescales, which is also apparent from their comparable autocorrelations shown in Figure 1H.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1H for example session

claim: On every one-chamber session, the difference component had smaller magnitudes than the mean component for 30–150 Hz LFP power.
source: The relationships seen in the one-chamber example above was robust: on every one-chamber session, the difference component had smaller magnitudes (Figure 1I) and faster timescales (Figure 1J) than the mean component (note that the relative magnitudes are a reflection of inter-brain correlation).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1I across all one-chamber sessions

claim: On every one-chamber session, the difference component had faster timescales than the mean component for 30–150 Hz LFP power.
source: The relationships seen in the one-chamber example above was robust: on every one-chamber session, the difference component had smaller magnitudes (Figure 1I) and faster timescales (Figure 1J) than the mean component (note that the relative magnitudes are a reflection of inter-brain correlation).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1J across all one-chamber sessions

claim: The relative magnitudes of the mean and difference components are a reflection of inter-brain correlation.
source: on every one-chamber session, the difference component had smaller magnitudes (Figure 1I) and faster timescales (Figure 1J) than the mean component (note that the relative magnitudes are a reflection of inter-brain correlation).
evidence: Mathematical relationship explained in Materials and methods

claim: On two-chambers sessions, the mean and difference components were comparable in magnitude and timescale for 30–150 Hz LFP power.
source: On two-chambers sessions, in contrast, the mean and difference were comparable (Figure 1K–L).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1K-L across all two-chambers sessions

claim: LFP power in the 30–150 Hz and 1–29 Hz bands, multiunits, and single units all showed the same significant trends in relative magnitudes and timescales of mean and difference components.
source: These relationships are summarized in Figure 1M–T for all four neural signals: LFP power in the 30–150 Hz and 1–29 Hz bands, multiunits, and single units all showed the same significant trends (see Figure 1—figure supplements 2–4 for examples and detailed results for 1–29 Hz LFP power, multiunits, and single units).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1M-T and figure supplements 2-4

claim: The inter-brain neural relationship during social interactions is characterized by two robust signatures: the relative magnitudes and relative timescales of the mean and difference components.
source: Thus, the inter-brain neural relationship during social interactions is characterized by two robust signatures of the mean and difference components: their relative magnitudes (which reflects inter-brain correlation) and their relative timescales.
evidence: Summary of experimental observations from Figure 1

claim: The observed relative magnitudes of mean and difference components are mathematically implied by the presence of inter-brain correlation.
source: As mentioned above, the observed relative magnitudes are mathematically implied by the presence of inter-brain correlation (Materials and methods).
evidence: Mathematical derivation provided in Materials and methods

claim: Having a given combination of correlation, mean component variance, and difference component variance does not place constraints on the timescales of the two components.
source: As we show in Materials and methods (section 'Surrogate data and the relationship between inter-brain correlation and mean and difference components'), the answer is no: having a given combination of correlation, mean component variance, and difference component variance does not place constraints on the timescales of the two components.
evidence: Demonstrated through mathematical analysis and surrogate data in Materials and methods and Figure 2

claim: Having a given combination of correlation, mean component variance, and difference component variance does not constrain the difference to be faster than the mean.
source: Specifically, it does not constrain the difference to be faster than the mean. To explicitly demonstrate this, we constructed a set of surrogate data as a counter-example (Figure 2).
evidence: Demonstrated through surrogate data shown in Figure 2

claim: Surrogate data with identical inter-brain correlation, mean component variance, and difference component variance as actual data can have difference components that are slower than the mean components.
source: The surrogate data was designed to have inter-brain correlation, mean component variance, and difference component variance that are identical to the actual data. However, unlike the actual data, the surrogate data was designed to have difference components that were slower than the mean components, the opposite of what was experimentally observed (Figure 2C and E).
evidence: Demonstrated through surrogate data shown in Figure 2

claim: The relative timescales of the difference and mean components are not dictated by their relative magnitudes or by inter-brain correlation.
source: Thus, the relative timescales of the difference and mean components are not dictated by their relative magnitudes or by inter-brain correlation.
evidence: Demonstrated through surrogate data analysis in Figure 2

claim: The model qualitatively reproduces the experimentally observed neural activity patterns including variability over time, modulation by behavior, and correlation across brains.
source: This model was used to simulate neural activity, which was then analyzed using the same methods used to analyze experimental data. The model qualitatively reproduces the experimentally observed neural activity patterns: simulated activity shows variability over time, modulation by behavior, and correlation across brains (Figure 3B; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for a quantitative comparison between model and data).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3B and figure supplement 1

claim: The model reproduces all the experimentally observed relationships between the magnitudes and timescales of the difference and mean components.
source: More importantly, the model also qualitatively reproduces all the experimentally observed relationships between the magnitudes and timescales of the difference and mean components, as can be seen in the activity and autocorrelation of the two components on an example simulation (Figure 3C–D). Specifically, the difference component had smaller magnitudes and faster timescales than the mean component in the one-chamber model, but not in the two-chambers model (Figure 3C–F).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3C-F

claim: In the model, functional across-brain coupling acts as negative feedback for the difference component, which suppresses the difference component while speeding it up.
source: On the other hand, functional across-brain coupling acts as negative feedback for the difference component, which suppresses the difference component while speeding it up (Figure 3H).
evidence: Derived from mathematical analysis of the model; illustrated in Figure 3H

claim: In the model, a single mechanism—opposite feedback (positive feedback to the mean component and negative feedback to the difference component)—contributes to all observations relating the magnitudes and timescales of the mean and difference components.
source: Thus, in the model, a single mechanism—opposite feedback, that is, positive feedback to the mean component and negative feedback to the difference component—contributes to all of our observations relating the magnitudes and timescales of the mean and difference components.
evidence: Derived from mathematical analysis of the model

claim: The tendency of bats to engage in the same behavior at the same time contributes to inter-brain correlation.
source: In the full version of our model, in addition to functional coupling, behavioral modulation also contributes to the inter-brain relationship (the effects of behavioral modulation are analyzed in depth in Materials and methods and Figure 3—figure supplement 2). In particular, the tendency of bats to engage in the same behavior at the same time (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G) contributes to inter-brain correlation.
evidence: Analyzed in Materials and methods and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2G

claim: After removing time periods of coordinated behavior from experimental sessions, inter-brain correlation persisted.
source: One specific experimental observation suggests that the answer is no: Figure 4A, B and G show that, after removing time periods of coordinated behavior from experimental sessions, inter-brain correlation persisted.
evidence: Shown in Figure 4A, B and G

claim: The model can reproduce the persistence of inter-brain correlation after removing time periods of coordinated behaviors.
source: We found that our model can reproduce this phenomenon (Figure 4C, D and G).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4C, D and G

claim: In the absence of functional across-brain coupling, inter-brain correlation disappeared after removing time periods of coordinated behaviors in the model.
source: Next, we simulated an alternative model with behavioral coordination, but without functional across-brain coupling (Materials and methods). Figure 4E–G show that, in the absence of functional across-brain coupling, inter-brain correlation disappeared after removing time periods of coordinated behaviors.
evidence: Shown in Figure 4E-G

claim: In the framework of the model, functional across-brain coupling is necessary to reproduce the experimental results.
source: Thus, in the framework of our model, functional across-brain coupling is necessary to reproduce the experimental results.
evidence: Demonstrated through comparison of models with and without functional across-brain coupling in Figure 4

claim: The Kuramoto model reproduces inter-brain correlation and the relative magnitudes of the mean and difference components from the data.
source: The Kuramoto model has been widely used to model diverse synchronization phenomena in physics, chemistry, and biology, including neural synchronization both within and across brains (e.g. Breakspear et al., 2010; Cumin and Unsworth, 2007; Dumas et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2015). Here, we adapted it to model inter-brain synchronization in bats. In this model, the fluctuating neural activity of the interacting bats are abstracted as oscillators whose phases are dynamically coupled depending on their phase difference (Materials and methods). This phase-coupling mechanism is able to reproduce inter-brain correlation and the relative magnitudes of the mean and difference components from the data; importantly, however, it does not reproduce the relative timescales of the mean and difference components from the data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The Kuramoto model does not reproduce the relative timescales of the mean and difference components from the data.
source: This phase-coupling mechanism is able to reproduce inter-brain correlation and the relative magnitudes of the mean and difference components from the data; importantly, however, it does not reproduce the relative timescales of the mean and difference components from the data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Not all forms of functional coupling are equally able to reproduce the inter-brain relationship.
source: This demonstrates that not all forms of functional coupling are equally able of reproducing the inter-brain relationship.
evidence: Demonstrated through comparison of main model and Kuramoto model in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The model predicts that correlation between neural activity variables mirrors the functional coupling strength as axes rotate.
source: In the one-chamber model, if we rotate the axes smoothly, the strength of functional coupling also changes smoothly (Figure 5A). In particular, the coupling strength is positive and at its maximum when the axes correspond to the activity of each bat, and it decreases to zero as the axes rotate by 45° (corresponding to the mean and difference components), and finally becoming negative as the axes rotate further (Figure 5A). After any amount of rotation, we can calculate the correlation between the activity variables. The model predicts that, as the axes rotate, the correlation between the neural activity variables would mirror the coupling strength (Figure 5B).
evidence: Model prediction shown in Figure 5A-B

claim: The data confirmed the model prediction that correlation as a function of rotation mirrors functional coupling strength.
source: As we turn back to the data, we found that it clearly confirmed the model predictions: correlation as a function of rotation showed the same relationship as in the model (Figure 5C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5C

claim: Data from two-chambers sessions confirmed the predictions of the two-chambers model showing near zero correlation across all axes rotation angles.
source: Similarly, data from the two-chambers sessions (Figure 5F) also confirmed the predictions of the two-chambers model (Figure 5D–E): namely, near zero correlation across all axes rotation angles.
evidence: Shown in Figure 5D-F

claim: The model predicts linear relationships between the variance ratio and centroid ratio across sessions.
source: This can be seen by plotting the relative magnitudes against the relative timescales for different simulations, which shows linear relationships between them (Figure 5G; see Materials and methods for detailed analysis of these relationships).
evidence: Model prediction shown in Figure 5G

claim: The data confirmed the model prediction of linear relationships between variance ratio and centroid ratio.
source: Turning to the data, we see similar linear relationships, again confirming the predictions of the model (Figure 5H).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5H

claim: In the model, the neural activity of each bat is directly modulated by its own behavior and indirectly modulated by the behavior of the other bat through functional across-brain coupling.
source: In the model, the neural activity of each bat is directly modulated by its own behavior; moreover, it is indirectly modulated by the behavior of the other bat, through functional across-brain coupling.
evidence: Derived from model structure

claim: The model predicts that the neural activity of each bat should represent the behavior of the other bat independently from encoding its own behavior.
source: This suggests that the neural activity of each bat should represent the behavior of the other bat independently from encoding its own behavior.
evidence: Model prediction derived from model structure

claim: The encoding of the other bat's behavior was significantly stronger for the one-chamber model than the two-chambers model.
source: Across simulations, we found that the encoding of the other bat's behavior was significantly stronger for the one-chamber model than the two-chambers model (Figure 6C), consistent with the presence of functional across-brain coupling in the one-chamber model.
evidence: Shown in Figure 6C

claim: In the data, the encoding of the other bat's behavior was stronger on one-chamber sessions than two-chambers sessions.
source: Applying the same approach to the data, we saw similar neural encoding of the other bat's behavior (example in Figure 6D, corresponding ROC curve in Figure 6E). Across all data sessions, the encoding was stronger on one-chamber sessions than two-chambers sessions, confirming the model predictions (Figure 6F).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6D-F

claim: The opposite feedback mechanism naturally generalizes to larger social groups.
source: First, can the opposite feedback mechanism be generalized to the larger group context? Second, what would such a mechanism predict about the group inter-brain relationship? To answer these questions, we extended our model to larger groups, which offered direct predictions regarding the group inter-brain relationship.
evidence: Demonstrated through extension of model to n-bat case

claim: Neural activity was simultaneously recorded from the frontal cortices of four bats while they interacted in a chamber.
source: Next, we tested these predictions using experimental data collected from a group of socially interacting bats. In this data set, neural activity was simultaneously and wirelessly recorded from the frontal cortices of four bats while they interacted in a chamber, under the same condition as the one-chamber sessions described above (Rose et al., 2021).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental method; supported by citation

claim: The 4-bat experimental data qualitatively confirmed all model predictions: activity patterns in the difference subspace had smaller magnitudes than the 4-bat mean component.
source: Applying the same analyses used for the 4-bat model simulations in Figure 7C–E, we found that the data qualitatively confirmed all model predictions: activity patterns in the difference subspace had smaller magnitudes (Figure 7F) and faster timescales (Figure 7G) than the 4-bat mean component, there was positive inter-brain correlation between bats in the group (Figure 7H), and there was no correlation between the 4-bat mean component and activity patterns in the difference subspace (Figure 7H).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7F

claim: The 4-bat experimental data qualitatively confirmed that activity patterns in the difference subspace had faster timescales than the 4-bat mean component.
source: Applying the same analyses used for the 4-bat model simulations in Figure 7C–E, we found that the data qualitatively confirmed all model predictions: activity patterns in the difference subspace had smaller magnitudes (Figure 7F) and faster timescales (Figure 7G) than the 4-bat mean component, there was positive inter-brain correlation between bats in the group (Figure 7H), and there was no correlation between the 4-bat mean component and activity patterns in the difference subspace (Figure 7H).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7G

claim: The 4-bat experimental data qualitatively confirmed that there was positive inter-brain correlation between bats in the group.
source: Applying the same analyses used for the 4-bat model simulations in Figure 7C–E, we found that the data qualitatively confirmed all model predictions: activity patterns in the difference subspace had smaller magnitudes (Figure 7F) and faster timescales (Figure 7G) than the 4-bat mean component, there was positive inter-brain correlation between bats in the group (Figure 7H), and there was no correlation between the 4-bat mean component and activity patterns in the difference subspace (Figure 7H).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7H

claim: The 4-bat experimental data qualitatively confirmed that there was no correlation between the 4-bat mean component and activity patterns in the difference subspace.
source: Applying the same analyses used for the 4-bat model simulations in Figure 7C–E, we found that the data qualitatively confirmed all model predictions: activity patterns in the difference subspace had smaller magnitudes (Figure 7F) and faster timescales (Figure 7G) than the 4-bat mean component, there was positive inter-brain correlation between bats in the group (Figure 7H), and there was no correlation between the 4-bat mean component and activity patterns in the difference subspace (Figure 7H).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7H

claim: The opposite feedback mechanism is not restricted to pair social interactions, but naturally generalizes to larger social groups.
source: In conclusion, we modeled the group inter-brain relationship and experimentally confirmed the model predictions. Through this, we found that the opposite feedback mechanism is not restricted to pair social interactions, but naturally generalizes to larger social groups.
evidence: Demonstrated through n-bat model and 4-bat experimental data in Figure 7

claim: Neural activity is correlated between the brains of socially interacting individuals in mice, bats, and humans.
source: First, it is well known that neural activity is correlated between the brains of socially interacting individuals, in mice, bats, and humans (e.g. Dikker et al., 2014; Kingsbury et al., 2019; Kinreich et al., 2017; Levy et al., 2017; Montague et al., 2002; Piazza et al., 2020; Spiegelhalder et al., 2014; Stolk et al., 2014; Zadbood et al., 2017; Zhang and Yartsev, 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature

claim: In a shared social environment, neural correlation across brains is above and beyond what would be expected from behavioral coordination between individuals.
source: Second, in a shared social environment, neural correlation across brains is above and beyond what would be expected from behavioral coordination between individuals (Kingsbury et al., 2019; Piazza et al., 2020; Zhang and Yartsev, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: The neural correlation between socially interacting individuals varies as a function of timescale: correlation across brains is higher for activity at slower timescales, and lower for activity at faster timescales.
source: Third, the neural correlation between socially interacting individuals varies as a function of timescale: correlation across brains is higher for activity at slower timescales, and lower for activity at faster timescales (Kingsbury et al., 2019; Zhang and Yartsev, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: The model offers a simple explanation for diverse aspects of the inter-brain neural relationship during both pair and group social interactions.
source: In summary, our model offers a particularly simple explanation for diverse aspects of the inter-brain neural relationship during both pair and group social interactions, including: (1) neural correlation across brains and the relative magnitudes of inter-brain mean and difference components (Figure 3E; Figure 7F and H); (2) neural correlation beyond behavioral coordination; (3) neural correlation as a function of timescale; (4) the relative timescales of inter-brain mean and difference components (Figure 3F; Figure 7G); (5) correlation between activity variables under rotated activity bases (Figure 5B–C); (6) the relationship between the magnitudes and timescales of activity components across sessions (Figure 5G–H); and (7) modulation of one bat's neural activity by the behavior of another bat (Figure 6).
evidence: Summary of model explanations supported by data in multiple figures

claim: The inter-brain relationship has been studied in three non-human species: bats, mice, and birds.
source: So far, this has been studied in three non-human species: bats, mice (Kingsbury et al., 2019), and birds (Hoffmann et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Bats and mice showed qualitatively similar inter-brain relationships.
source: While bats and mice showed qualitatively similar inter-brain relationships, birds were different, showing anti-correlated neural activity across brains during a duetting behavior (Hoffmann et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on comparison to prior literature

claim: Birds showed anti-correlated neural activity across brains during a duetting behavior.
source: While bats and mice showed qualitatively similar inter-brain relationships, birds were different, showing anti-correlated neural activity across brains during a duetting behavior (Hoffmann et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: Data was collected from eight adult male Egyptian fruit bats (Rousettus aegyptiacus).
source: Data was collected from eight adult male Egyptian fruit bats (Rousettus aegyptiacus).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental subjects

claim: All procedures were approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee of UC Berkeley.
source: All procedures were approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee of UC Berkeley.
evidence: Direct statement of ethical approval

claim: Experiments were conducted inside 40.6 × 33.7 × 52.1 cm cages placed in dark chambers.
source: Experiments were conducted inside 40.6 × 33.7 × 52.1 cm (length × width × height) cages, placed in dark chambers.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental setup

claim: High-speed infrared video cameras were used to record videos of the bats.
source: High-speed infrared video cameras (Flea3 or Chameleon3, FLIR) were used to record videos of the bats, and ultrasonic microphones (USG Electret Ultrasound Microphone, Avisoft Bioacoustics) were used to record audio.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental equipment

claim: Ultrasonic microphones were used to record audio.
source: High-speed infrared video cameras (Flea3 or Chameleon3, FLIR) were used to record videos of the bats, and ultrasonic microphones (USG Electret Ultrasound Microphone, Avisoft Bioacoustics) were used to record audio.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental equipment

claim: The behaviors of the bats were manually annotated by experienced observers.
source: For the two-bat experiments, the behaviors of the bats were manually annotated by experienced observers.
evidence: Direct statement of data processing method

claim: Bats were implanted with four-tetrode microdrives to target the frontal cortex.
source: Anesthesia and surgery were performed as described previously in Yartsev and Ulanovsky, 2013 to implant the bats with four-tetrode microdrives (Harlan 4 Drive, Neuralynx). To target the frontal cortex, the center of craniotomy was positioned at 1.7 mm lateral to the midline and 12.19 mm anterior to the transverse sinus located between cortex and cerebellum.
evidence: Direct statement of surgical procedure; supported by citation

claim: Electrophysiology was performed using a wireless neural data logging system.
source: Electrophysiology was performed using a wireless neural data logging system (Neurolog-16 and MouseLog-16, Deuteron Technologies).
evidence: Direct statement of recording equipment

claim: Tetrodes were advanced ventrally every one to two days to record activity at different sites.
source: Tetrodes were advanced ventrally every one to two days (mostly by 20–160 µm), to record activity at different sites.
evidence: Direct statement of recording procedure

claim: Histology was performed using Nissl staining to determine neural recording sites.
source: To determine the neural recording sites, we performed histology as previously described (Yartsev and Ulanovsky, 2013), using Nissl staining.
evidence: Direct statement of histological method; supported by citation

claim: LFP was obtained by low-pass filtering the raw voltage traces with a cut-off frequency of 200 Hz and downsampling to 496.6 Hz or 520.8 Hz.
source: To obtain LFP, we low-pass filtered the raw voltage traces (cut-off frequency: 200 Hz), and then downsampled it to 496.6 Hz (the two-bat experiments) or 520.8 Hz (the four-bat experiments).
evidence: Direct statement of data processing method

claim: Spikes were detected from band-pass filtered (600–6000 Hz) voltage traces using threshold crossing.
source: We detected spikes from band-pass filtered (600–6000 Hz) voltage traces using threshold crossing.
evidence: Direct statement of data processing method

claim: Spike sorting was done automatically using SNAP Sorter, then manually checked using SpikeSort3D.
source: Spike sorting was done automatically using SNAP Sorter (Neuralynx), then manually checked using SpikeSort3D (Neuralynx).
evidence: Direct statement of data processing method

claim: All units with firing rate below 2 Hz were excluded from further analysis.
source: All units with firing rate below 2 Hz were excluded from further analysis.
evidence: Direct statement of data processing criterion

claim: LFP spectrograms were calculated using the multitaper method for 5 s sliding windows with 2.5 s overlap between consecutive windows.
source: To calculate LFP spectrograms, power spectra were calculated using the multitaper method for 5 s sliding windows of the LFP trace, with 2.5 s overlap between consecutive windows.
evidence: Direct statement of data processing method

claim: Firing rates for single units and multiunits were computed in 5 s bins with 2.5 s overlap between consecutive bins.
